title: Would you actually trust an AI agent with $10k of your portfolio?
author: Arpitbuilds
selftext:
Hey guys, I genuinely want feedback here! If you had an AI trading agent with a good track record, would you actually let it manage $10k completely on its own and actually sleep peacefully?

I'm less interested in the trading strategy and more in the trust/security side. For anyone already running autonomous trading agents, what guardrails do you actually have in place today? Spend limits, approvals, restricted actions, something else?

asking because we're building something around agent security and want to understand where people's heads are at. if anyone's already using some kind of security/guardrail setup for their trading agent, would love to hear details, the more specific the better.

comments.author: joshman1204
comments.body: I've been running agents with atleast $10k of real money invested for the past 3 months. Lost a few hundred in the early days to some dumb mistakes but otherwise it's going ok. I'm slowly increasing the amount of money I let the agent control it started at $1k and is now at $10k and will most likely be moving to $25k on Aug 1st unless I get brave and skip to $50k. Goal is low six figures in agentic trades by the end of the year.

comments.body: I've seen way more than 10k lol, I've seen people with 50k on Cod3x, and it worked out great for him.

comments.author: DustDirect2997
comments.body:
Not with complete control. Josh's split—LLM proposes, deterministic code validates and executes—is the right boundary. I’d add portfolio-wide limits and failure tests, because a per-order calculator can still approve a dangerous cluster.



My minimum control plane:



1. Scope: the model can propose, never withdraw or transfer. Allowlist venue, symbol, side and order type.

2. Hard limits outside the prompt: max loss per trade, gross exposure, correlated concentration, leverage and daily drawdown.

3. State checks: reject stale prices/account data; read canonical broker state; require idempotency keys and duplicate-order locks.

4. Independent execution check: recompute size, stop distance, margin and expected slippage outside the model. Require human approval above a fixed notional or for any new venue/model version.

5. Audit and recovery: persist the evidence, model/prompt version, proposal, rule verdict and broker receipt; reconcile broker state on a timer; keep a kill switch.



Before trusting it, deliberately submit an oversized instruction, stale input, duplicate order and correlated-exposure breach. All four should fail closed. Also paper-track every rejected trade to the same exit horizon as accepted trades; otherwise fewer trades can masquerade as a better filter.



The model proposes. Code sizes, approves or rejects. And if the same model writes and grades the trade, that is still one control, not two.



Disclosure: I help run Clash of AIs, an educational simulated multi-model comparison. We treat model disagreement as a risk signal, not a confidence vote. Educational only; no return promise.

comments.author: Good_Character_20
comments.body: The distinction that matters most is where the limit lives. A spend cap written into the prompt is a suggestion, since the model can reason its way around it or simply lose it somewhere in a long context. The same cap enforced in the execution layer is a constraint, because the agent never gets to have an opinion about it. So the guardrails worth having are the ones the agent cannot see or argue with. Position size and daily loss checked at order submission rather than in the system prompt, broker keys held somewhere the agent has no read access to, and a paper mode that takes a human action to leave rather than a flag the agent can set itself. If a guardrail only works because the model agreed to it, it is not a guardrail.

comments.author: Interesting_Gold_792
comments.body:
I wouldn't go from paper trading straight to trusting an agent with $10k.

I'm building my own automated system and I'm still in paper testing. The more I've worked on it, the more I've realized that the strategy itself is only part of the trust problem.

Before I'd trust it with meaningful money, I want things like persistent position state, duplicate-trade protection, stale/missing data checks, clear risk limits, an execution ledger, safe recovery after restarts, and a hard separation between paper and live execution.

My plan is to run it against live market data without allowing execution first, then move to very small live trades and compare what actually happens with what the paper system expected.

If it can't behave correctly with a tiny amount of real money, there's no reason I'd trust it with $10k.
